markets.note: Miners, led by uranium stocks, lifted the ASX while ANZ fell 3.2% and dragged the banks; overnight attention turns to Nvidia, whose shares are sliding on the Jensen Huang spy scandal.

lead.headline: Russia, Ukraine, and the US meet in Abu Dhabi as both sides hit energy targets
lead.body: Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine, and the United States sit down in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for two days of talks, the first round since February, with security guarantees expected to top the agenda. On the eve of the talks Ukrainian drones set Russia's Kirishi refinery alight, while Russia said it struck three Ukrainian power substations. Russia still wants Ukraine out of four annexed regions and off the NATO path; Ukraine wants a ceasefire first.
lead.why: Any movement on security guarantees would be the first real sign of a framework to end Europe's biggest war, with knock-on effects for energy prices and defence spending.
points: Two-day talks start Tuesday 10 November in Abu Dhabi.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says post-war security guarantees are the key focus.
Ukraine is short of US-made Patriot interceptors as Russia targets the power grid before winter.

lead.headline: Trump meets Qatar's prime minister as Iran pitches a two-day peace plan
lead.body: Donald Trump is meeting Qatar's Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, at the White House as Doha tries to restart US-Iran negotiations. Iran has offered a revised two-day framework: Washington would act on agreed measures on day one, and the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on day two. Rubio says Iran's demands, including lifting the US port blockade and sanctions and paying war compensation, are unacceptable and no breakthrough is imminent.
lead.why: The Iran war has kept Brent near US$100, fed the inflation behind this year's rate hikes, and helped sink Trump's party at the midterms.
points: Iran will not discuss its nuclear program until its conditions are met.
Trump says new strikes are 'highly unlikely' if talks progress but warns more targets have been identified.
Qatar has warned against letting talks drag on indefinitely.

lead.headline: COP31 opens in Türkiye with Chris Bowen running the negotiations
lead.body: The UN climate summit opened in Antalya on Monday, and for the first time Australia is chairing the formal negotiations, with Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen as President of Negotiations while Türkiye hosts. Bowen inherits a long list of issues deferred from June's Bonn session, including carbon market rules, adaptation indicators, a just transition mechanism, and climate finance. Scientists expect 2026 to be the hottest year on record.
lead.why: Bowen's handling of the talks will shape Australia's standing in the Pacific and put its gas and coal exports under a bright international spotlight.
points: A Pacific pre-COP in Fiji and Tuvalu backed electricity supplying 35% of global final energy by 2035.
More than 160 agenda items are on the table.

lead.headline: Big Build royal commission hears CFMEU had 'unprecedented access' to Victorian ministers
lead.body: Public hearings in the royal commission into the CFMEU and Victoria's Big Build began on Monday, with counsel assisting Chris Young KC tabling John Holland memos describing the union's 'unprecedented access' to ministers. The first day examined a 2022 stop-work at a Sunbury level crossing site, where transcript notes recorded the union warning it would 'smash' a subcontractor. Premier Ben Carroll denied knowledge of the union's access and said the hearings showed he would make tough decisions.
lead.why: The hearings run until 20 November, eight days before a state election in which Labor is already polling at record lows.
points: Counsel stressed the material is allegations, some of which are denied.
The Sunbury project cost reportedly blew out by about $6 million.
The commission has requested more than 110,000 documents.

lead.headline: Nvidia shares slide as its board investigates Jensen Huang over a suspected Chinese spy
lead.body: Nvidia's independent directors have launched an investigation after the New York Times and Financial Times reported US officials believed a Singapore-based executive with a close relationship to CEO Jensen Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset. Huang admitted an affair in a staff memo and remains CEO; the board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China called the claims 'smears', and Nvidia shares fell more than 4%.
lead.why: Nvidia is the world's most valuable company and a top holding in global index ETFs, so a leadership crisis there feeds straight into diversified portfolios.
points: The woman worked at Megaspeed, a Nvidia customer.
The NYT reported Trump was briefed about a year ago.
The scandal lands as markets were already rethinking the AI trade after the midterms.

items.headline: Watt tells Labor colleagues to stop undermining Chalmers
items.body: Environment Minister Murray Watt has urged colleagues to stop briefing against the Treasurer after a budget savings meeting, saying 'all sorts of people' were 'making all sorts of comments'.
items.why: Open sniping at the Treasurer after five rate hikes is a sign of how rattled federal Labor has become.

items.headline: Minns calls One Nation candidate's 'replacement' claim racist
items.body: Premier Chris Minns and the Race Discrimination Commissioner condemned Stuart Bonds, who leads One Nation's NSW upper house ticket, for claiming Australians are being 'demographically replaced'.

items.headline: WA minister under pressure over Pilbara child welfare crisis
items.body: Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch visited South Hedland for the first time since reports of children living in squalid conditions, as calls for his resignation grow.

items.headline: Tasmanian premier takes 22% pay rise he once called 'out of step'
items.body: All Tasmanian MPs, including the premier, are now receiving the full 22 per cent increase.

items.headline: Demerit point black markets outpace a 1990s system
items.body: After 7.30 exposed demerit points being traded on social media, the official who introduced Queensland's system says the government must change it.

items.headline: Trump concedes deportations were 'too tough' as Miller becomes chief of staff
items.body: Trump told 60 Minutes his deportation policy hurt him at the midterms and floated an immigration deal with Democrats, even as Stephen Miller, its chief architect, replaced Susie Wiles as chief of staff.
items.why: It is the clearest sign yet that the midterm defeat is changing White House policy, not just personnel.

items.headline: Krakow gunman dies in hospital
items.body: The 24-year-old who killed six people and injured 15 in Krakow's Main Market Square has died; Poland is still investigating the attack as terrorism and whether he acted alone.

items.headline: Winter rains flood Gaza's tent camps
items.body: Gaza authorities blamed global 'inaction' after a sandbank collapsed onto a tent in heavy rain, killing four children and a woman.

items.headline: At least 34 dead as migrant boat sinks off Senegal
items.body: The boat was attempting the dangerous Atlantic crossing to Spain's Canary Islands.

items.headline: Sheikh Hasina seeks a passport in sign of Bangladesh return
items.body: The ousted prime minister, in India for two years, has promised to return home.

items.headline: Uranium stocks surge as miners carry the ASX
items.body: Paladin and Boss Energy jumped more than 10% and BHP rose 2.4%, offsetting losses across the big banks as the ASX 200 closed 0.1% higher at about 9,030.
items.why: A market held up by miners while banks fall is the pattern to watch for Australian-heavy ETFs like VDHG.

items.headline: US futures point higher despite the Nvidia scandal
items.body: S&P 500 futures were up 0.7% and Nasdaq futures 0.6% in the Australian afternoon.

items.headline: UK to cut its electric vehicle sales targets
items.body: The UK government is expected this week to water down targets that phase out new petrol and diesel cars by 2030.

items.headline: Thames Water asks creditors for more time on £20b debt
items.body: The troubled utility wants part of its debt deadline pushed out to March 2028.

items.headline: Mickleham auction beats reserve by $40,000 days after a rate hike
items.body: Four bidders pushed a house in Melbourne's north well above expectations, defying this month's RBA increase.
items.why: Pockets of outer-suburban demand are holding up even as higher rates cool clearance rates elsewhere.

items.headline: Canberra plans a new 3,000-home suburb
items.body: Residents are being asked what matters most for a new suburb in the city's north-west.

items.headline: Adult children have a say in most downsizing decisions
items.body: A new report finds two in three downsizers say their kids influence the move.

items.headline: NEJM: plozasiran cuts pancreatitis in severe hypertriglyceridaemia
items.body: In the SHASTA-3 and SHASTA-4 trials (n=757), the APOC3-targeting siRNA cut triglycerides by about 80% at 12 months and acute pancreatitis from 5 to 1 per 100 patient-years (rate ratio 0.22). Takeaway: APOC3 silencing now has outcome data on pancreatitis, not just lipid lowering; the first author is based in Perth.
items.why: It moves severe hypertriglyceridaemia treatment from lowering a number to preventing a dangerous admission.

items.headline: NEJM: community CPR push fails to lift cardiac arrest survival
items.body: A county-randomised North Carolina trial of 22,459 out-of-hospital arrests combined dispatcher, first-responder AED, and community CPR training but did not improve survival with good neurological outcome. Takeaway: bystander CPR rates rose late, so the effect may need a longer, Denmark-style program.

items.headline: NEJM: retatrutide delivers about 24% weight loss with joint and sleep benefits
items.body: In TRIUMPH-1 (n=2,339), the triple agonist cut body weight 23.7% at 9 mg and 25.0% at 12 mg versus 3.9% on placebo at 80 weeks, and reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and the apnoea-hypopnoea index. Takeaway: GI effects were most common; expect it to reset the obesity drug benchmark.

items.headline: Draft telehealth standards target commercial influence on prescribing
items.body: The Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care wants virtual care executives to ensure treatment decisions are free from commercial influence, with summaries sent to a patient's regular GP.

items.headline: Victoria's GP ADHD directory sent patients to closed books
items.body: At least 15 listed services were not accepting new patients.

items.headline: Cannabis-related admissions in Victoria up 49%
items.body: Researchers are calling for public health measures as hospital admissions linked to cannabis rise.

items.headline: Vaccine trial against Bundibugyo virus begins
items.body: The Tumaini trial is testing candidate vaccines against Bundibugyo, an ebolavirus with no licensed vaccine.
items.why: Current Ebola vaccines target the Zaire strain, leaving outbreaks of this species without a preventive tool.

items.headline: The super El Niño is a health shock as well as a climate one
items.body: Nature argues heat, disease, and food insecurity from the event need health systems at the centre of planning.

items.headline: How AI transformed mathematics
items.body: Nature traces how AI tools moved from curiosity to a working part of mathematical research.

items.headline: Parkes baby born at 32 weeks now thriving
items.body: Maelie spent 86 days in hospital in Sydney and Orange after her lungs collapsed early; 18 months on, her mum says 'you wouldn't even know'.
items.why: A reminder of how far regional families still travel for neonatal care.

items.headline: Peter McDonald Premiership clubs make early 2027 signings
items.body: Several clubs have already landed statement recruits in the off-season.

opinion.title: Both worse and better
opinion.author: Michael Jacobs
opinion.gist: Warming is accelerating, but cheap electrification offers a real path that COP31's formal talks largely ignore.

opinion.title: The Philippines is looking to develop an "expeditionary navy"
opinion.author: Vincent Kyle Parada
opinion.gist: Manila wants a blue-water navy, but its frigates lack weapons and its fleet lacks fuel to go far.

opinion.title: The point-scoring over the Krakow shooting has already begun
opinion.author: Bartek Staniszewski
opinion.gist: Polish politicians rushed to weaponise the attack before the facts were known.

opinion.title: Keir Starmer is wrong to think Nato is unsalvageable
opinion.author: Eliot Wilson
opinion.gist: Europe should build up its own defence co-operation inside the alliance rather than give up on it.

opinion.title: We can't just 'move on': Democrats must hold Trump accountable
opinion.author: Jan-Werner Müller
opinion.gist: The new Congress must end the culture of political impunity rather than turn the page.

opinion.title: Today's AI won't achieve superintelligence. But catastrophic risk is real
opinion.author: Sunita Verma
opinion.gist: The same technical limits that rule out superintelligence make current systems dangerous, and we know how to manage that.

stories.headline: Kangaroos thump Samoa to set up a trans-Tasman final
stories.body: Australia beat Samoa 44 to 12 before 41,259 fans at Allianz Stadium and will meet New Zealand in Sunday's final in Brisbane; Samoa's Spencer Leniu copped a two-match ban for a money gesture at referees.

stories.headline: Cameron Bruce named Brisbane Lions coach
stories.body: The Lions went in-house to replace three-time premiership coach Chris Fagan with his long-time assistant.

tidbit: COP31 is the first UN climate conference where Australia chairs the formal negotiations, under a deal that has Türkiye hosting the summit while Chris Bowen runs the talks.

chapters.title: Welcome
chapters.text: Good evening Chris, and welcome to your evening briefing for Monday the ninth of November. Tonight: Russia, Ukraine, and the United States head back to the table in Abu Dhabi. Donald Trump meets Qatar's prime minister as Iran pitches a two-day peace plan. The big UN climate summit opens in Türkiye, with an Australian running the talks. Victoria's royal commission into the construction union goes public, three weeks out from the state election. And a spy scandal hits the world's most valuable company, Nvidia. Then a quick lap of the world, the markets, some big new trials in medicine, and news from around the Central West.

chapters.title: Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
chapters.text: First, the war in Ukraine. Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine, and the United States sit down in Abu Dhabi tomorrow for two days of talks. It's the first round since February, and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says security guarantees for Ukraine after the war will be the main focus. Neither side has softened much. Russia still wants Ukraine to pull out of four regions it claims to have annexed, give up on joining NATO, and accept limits on its military. Ukraine refuses to cede territory and wants a ceasefire first. Both sides spent the eve of the talks hitting energy targets. Ukrainian drones set fire to the Kirishi refinery near Saint Petersburg, Russia's second biggest, and a local woman was killed by falling debris. Russia says it struck three Ukrainian power substations, part of a campaign against the grid as winter arrives, while Ukraine runs short of Patriot interceptors. Expectations are low, but any agreed shape for security guarantees would be the first real step toward a framework for peace.

chapters.title: Iran and Qatar
chapters.text: Next, the Iran war. Donald Trump is meeting Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, at the White House as Doha tries to restart talks between Washington and Tehran. Iran has put forward a revised two-day plan. On day one, the United States would act on agreed measures, and on day two, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen to shipping. But Iran's list of conditions is long: ending the American blockade of its ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing assets, and compensation for war damage. Marco Rubio calls those demands unacceptable and says no breakthrough is close. Trump says new strikes are highly unlikely if talks progress, but warns more targets have been identified. Why does this matter here? Because this war has kept oil near a hundred US dollars a barrel, fed the inflation behind this year's interest rate hikes, and played a big part in Trump's midterm losses.

chapters.title: COP31 opens with Australia in the chair
chapters.text: Now to climate. The COP31 summit opened today in Antalya, in Türkiye, and it is a first for Australia. Under a deal struck last year, Türkiye hosts the conference, but Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen is President of Negotiations, meaning he chairs the formal talks. He has a heavy in-tray, with plenty of hard questions pushed over from June's session in Bonn: rules for carbon markets, how to measure adaptation, a mechanism for a just transition, and money for developing countries. Pacific nations, who hosted a pre-summit in Fiji and Tuvalu last month, backed a goal of electricity supplying thirty five per cent of the world's energy by twenty thirty five. All of this happens as scientists predict this will be the hottest year on record. Bowen will also face questions about Australia's own coal and gas exports. The talks run until the twentieth of November.

chapters.title: The Big Build royal commission
chapters.text: In Victoria, the royal commission into the construction union and the state's Big Build infrastructure program held its first public hearing today. Counsel assisting, Chris Young KC, tabled memos from the builder John Holland describing what it called the union's unprecedented access to ministers. The first case study was a twenty twenty two stop-work at a level crossing removal site in Sunbury, where notes recorded the union warning it would smash a subcontractor. Counsel was careful to say these are allegations, and some are denied. Premier Ben Carroll says he had no knowledge of the union's access and that the hearings show he will make tough decisions. The politics are brutal, though. These hearings run until the twentieth of November, just eight days before Victorians vote, with Labor polling at record lows.

chapters.title: Nvidia's spy scandal
chapters.text: Our fifth story is about money, and possibly your money. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom and the world's most valuable company, has launched an independent investigation into its chief executive, Jensen Huang. The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that American officials believed a Singapore-based executive, who had a close relationship with Huang, was working for Chinese intelligence. Huang has admitted an affair in a memo to staff and apologised, but remains in charge. The board says it has no reason to think national security or company secrets were compromised, and China calls the claims smears. Nvidia shares fell more than four per cent. Because Nvidia is one of the biggest holdings in global index funds, a crisis there flows straight through to diversified portfolios like yours.

chapters.title: Around the world
chapters.text: A quick lap of the world. Donald Trump has told the program Sixty Minutes that his deportation policy was too tough and hurt him at the midterms, and he's open to an immigration deal with Democrats. Yet he has just promoted Stephen Miller, the architect of that policy, to chief of staff. In Poland, the twenty four year old gunman who killed six people in Krakow's main square has died in hospital, and the terrorism investigation continues. Winter rain has flooded tent camps in Gaza, where a collapsing sandbank killed four children and a woman. At least thirty four people have died after a migrant boat sank off Senegal, heading for the Canary Islands. And closer to home, Environment Minister Murray Watt has told his Labor colleagues to stop undermining Treasurer Jim Chalmers, a sign of how rattled the government is after five rate rises. In New South Wales, Premier Chris Minns has called comments by One Nation's lead upper house candidate, Stuart Bonds, outrageous and racist, after Bonds claimed Australians are being demographically replaced. And in Western Australia, Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch is facing calls to resign over reports of children living in squalid conditions in South Hedland.

chapters.title: Markets
chapters.text: To the markets. The ASX two hundred finished the day up a tenth of one per cent at about nine thousand and thirty. Miners did the heavy lifting, with uranium stocks Paladin and Boss Energy up more than ten per cent and BHP up two point four. The banks went the other way, led by ANZ, which fell more than three per cent despite a profit of seven point three billion dollars. The Australian dollar is buying just under sixty nine US cents. Brent crude is flat around ninety eight dollars a barrel, gold is up one point four per cent to about four thousand one hundred and twenty US dollars an ounce, and Bitcoin is near seventy four and a half thousand. The cash rate stays at four point eight five per cent after five hikes this year. Overnight, watch Nvidia.

chapters.title: Health and medicine
chapters.text: In medicine, three trials worth knowing. In the New England Journal, the SHASTA three and four trials tested plozasiran, a small interfering RNA against apolipoprotein C three, in seven hundred and fifty seven adults with severe hypertriglyceridaemia. Triglycerides fell by about eighty per cent, and acute pancreatitis dropped from five to one per hundred patient years, with a Perth researcher as first author. Also in the journal, a large North Carolina trial found that training dispatchers, first responders, and communities in CPR did not improve survival after cardiac arrest, though bystander CPR rates did rise late in the study. And the triple agonist retatrutide produced around twenty four per cent weight loss at eighty weeks, with less knee pain and fewer apnoeas. Closer to home, draft national telehealth standards would require virtual clinics to keep prescribing free from commercial influence.

chapters.title: Dubbo and the Central West
chapters.text: Around the Central West, a lovely story from Parkes. Teagan's daughter Maelie was born at thirty two weeks after a difficult pregnancy, spent eighty six days in hospital between Sydney and Orange, and is now thriving at eighteen months. And in the Peter McDonald Premiership, clubs are already making early signings for twenty twenty seven.

chapters.title: Sign-off
chapters.text: In sport, the Kangaroos thumped Samoa forty four to twelve and meet New Zealand in Sunday's World Cup final in Brisbane, with the Jillaroos also facing New Zealand earlier that afternoon. That's your evening briefing, Chris. Your morning edition lands at six tomorrow, with the first day of the Abu Dhabi talks and how Wall Street took the Nvidia news. Have a good night.
